notes.1: It is important in the study of AS Level Chemistry that candidates are able to describe and explain the major trends in the chemistry of the elements of the third period of the Periodic Table. In this question there were many good answers to all parts of the question. However, some candidates’ answers were marred by the lack of a clear explanation when it was required.
notes.1a: (i) The majority of candidates correctly stated that from Na to Cl there are more protons in the nucleus. Fewer stated clearly that this gives an increased nuclear attraction for electrons. Fewer still explained that from Na to Cl the electrons are in the same shell and experience the same shielding.
notes.1aii: This was very well answered by many candidates who explained that argon exists as a monatomic gas which does not form any compounds. The statements ‘argon is a noble gas’ or ‘argon is inert’ were not accepted as explanations.
notes.1b: (i) Almost all candidates retrieved the correct data from the Data Booklet.
notes.1bii: This part was less well answered. It was expected that candidates would compare the numbers of electrons in the cation with those in the parent atom and explain that the greater number of protons would pull the remaining electrons closer to the nucleus. Some candidates did this in terms of all of the electrons in the outer shell of an atom being removed to form the corresponding cation.
notes.1iii: This part was less well done with many equations containing simple errors. Typical examples of incorrect answers were the following equations which appeared quite often. NaOH + H SO → Na SO + H O 2 3 2 3 2 2NaOH + H SO → Na SO + H O 2 3 2 4 2
notes.1c: (i) There were many correct equations for both oxides but a significant number of candidates gave unbalanced equations or gave an incorrect product. The most common of these was the production of H SO in the reaction of SO with H O. 2 4 2 2
notes.1cii: Correct values of pH were given by most candidates.
notes.2: The ability to work through a sequence of calculations, such as those in this question, is important in both the theory and the practical parts of AS Level Chemistry. There were many correct answers to this question with candidates demonstrating good mathematical skills in working through the problem. Those candidates who were unable to obtain the correct value of x in Na CO .xH O usually had a very unstructured and illogical approach to the calculation. 2 3 2
notes.2a: (i) This was generally correctly answered although a small number of candidates gave unbalanced equations.
notes.2aii: The majority of candidates gave a correct answer to this part.
notes.2iii: This too was well answered by most candidates.
notes.2iv: Again, a large number of candidates answered this correctly.
notes.2v: There were fewer correct answers to this part, with a number of candidates giving a wrong value for M of Na CO , either by using proton numbers rather than values of A or by arithmetical error. r 2 3 r
notes.2b: A significant number of candidates struggled with this part. Some did not know how to use the answers they had calculated in part (a), while others used wrong data or made arithmetical errors.
notes.3: Questions that relate to chemical thermodynamics need to be answered carefully and accurately. Answers must not be ambiguous. While there were many good responses to this question, there were also many candidates who lost credit through a lack of care with definitions or calculations.
notes.3a: Many equations were incorrect because they were unbalanced, because they lacked state symbols, or because the latter were wrong. With regard to state symbols, many candidates incorrectly gave H O(g) instead of H O(l) for water 2 2 at 298 K. A small number gave CH OCH (l) despite information in the question that DME is a gas. 3 3 A small number of candidates wrote an equation in terms of 2CH OCH which cannot be used for 3 3 the enthalpy change of combustion of one mole of CH OCH . 3 3 Definitions of ∆Ho were often insufficiently rigorous and sometimes extremely vague. It was expected that the definition would begin with a phrase such as ‘the enthalpy change of combustion is the enthalpy change when...’. Statements which began ‘it is when 1 mol of...’ were not accepted. Definitions that referred to ‘...the energy required to...’ were not accepted because combustion is always exothermic.
notes.3b: While many candidates obtained the correct answer, there were still many who did not. The most common error was to overlook the two moles of CH OH in the equation; Some candidates calculated the value of ∆Ho for the reverse reaction. reaction Candidates were asked to include a sign in their answer; a significant number did not do this and were penalised. A small number of candidates used bond energy data from the Data Booklet and received no credit for their answers.
notes.3c: (i) Most candidates drew two correct displayed formulae. One common error was to show the hydroxyl group in ethanol as O–H–C rather than H–O–C. A small number of candidates drew two structures for ethanol that, at first sight, appeared to be different.
notes.3cii: This was correctly answered by many candidates.
notes.3d: (i) There were fewer correct answers to this part with ‘van der Waals’ forces’ a common wrong response.
notes.3dii: Many candidates drew very good clear diagrams which showed, as the question required, the relevant dipoles and lone pairs. Some candidates failed to show the dipole on one –O–H bond, putting the δ+ and δ– charges on atoms in two separate molecules instead. A number of candidates also lost credit for failing to show clearly that the hydrogen bond exists between the lone pair of an oxygen atom in one ethanol molecule and the hydrogen atom of the –OH group in another ethanol molecule.
notes.4: Knowledge of the organic chemistry that is examined at AS Level is only gained by learning the relevant material. Candidates’ performance in this question suggests that many candidates have worked hard to learn the chemistry because answers were, in general, better than those seen in last year’s examination. However, there were still candidates who clearly had not done the necessary learning.
notes.4a: The majority of answers to this part were correct.
notes.4b: Many correct equations were given in answer to this part. A small number of candidates received no credit because their equations contained hydrogen or were unbalanced.
notes.4c: Many candidates scored well in this part with the structural formulae of correct compounds clearly shown. This was particularly true for compounds B and C. There were fewer correct answers for compound A which was frequently shown as ethanal rather than ethanoic acid. Answers for compound D were the least well done with candidates giving some very strange looking oxidation products such as CH CH CH CH and CH CHOCHOCH . 3 2 2 3 3 3
notes.4d: (i) This was well answered by many candidates.
notes.4dii: Fewer candidates were able to deduce the identities of the two compounds, B and C, that were chiral.
notes.4e: This was quite well answered but some candidates gave structures which contained 5-valent carbon atoms.
notes.4f: (i) This part tested candidates’ ability to apply familiar reactions to compounds they probably had not encountered before. There were some very good answers.
notes.4fii: Most of the candidates who had stated that buta-1,3-diene was produced in part (i) gave the correct tetrabromo- derivative in this part.
notes.4iii: This was generally well answered although some candidates confused electrophilic and nucleophilic addition.
notes.5: Although this question included a somewhat unusual calculation, there were many good answers. As with earlier questions, the structural formulae produced by some candidates were not always clearly drawn.
notes.5a: (i) The majority of candidates correctly identified the gas G as CO .
notes.5aii: This too was generally well answered with candidates identifying the functional group present in F as a carboxylic acid group. The answer ‘acid’ was not accepted because this could refer to any acid such as hydrochloric.
notes.5b: (i) Although ‘oxidation’ was the most common wrong answer, most candidates gave a correct response to this part.
notes.5bii: From the information given in the question, many candidates realised that compound H was a carboxylic acid which also contained a >C=C< bond. However there were many wrong answers most of which showed that candidates did not know the use of cold dilute acidified KMnO as a test for an alkene. A small number thought that a cyclic ester would be formed.
notes.5c: Many candidates struggled with this part, often because they did not adopt a logical approach to the problem. From the information given in the question it can be shown that compound F contains one –OH group and one –CO H group. Thus one mole of F produces one mole of H when reacted with an 2 2 excess of Na. Some candidates explained this by means of a chemical equation.
notes.5d: (i) Many candidates were able to draw at least one structural formula of the isomers of compound F.
notes.5dii: This part was quite well answered. The most common incorrect answer was to give an aldehyde for the oxidation product of F, despite the compound being heated under reflux with acidified K Cr O . 2 2 7

notes.general_comments:
This paper tested the candidates’ knowledge and understanding of important aspects of AS Level Chemistry.
The overall standard achieved by candidates was somewhat improved compared to last year, with an
encouraging performance in the calculation questions. Most candidates showed some positive achievement.
